comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological claims (C1, C2, C55, C56, C102-C109). Both evaluations find the experimental design, sample size, and procedures well-documented and appropriate. Reviewers note methods are 'well-written' with 'clear' figures, aligning with OpenEval's assessment of consistent and detailed documentation.

Perfect agreement on core revaluation finding (C9-C11). Both evaluations affirm the temporal dependency evidence from repeated-pair analysis. Reviewers explicitly state authors 'provide convincing evidence that subjective values change across sequences' and 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon,' matching OpenEval's assessment of converging evidence with appropriate statistical testing.

Perfect agreement on model comparison claims (C13-C17). Both evaluations support that d-values outperform s-values in explaining choice and RT data. Reviewers describe evidence as 'solid' and methods as 'novel' and 'robust,' affirming that dynamic valuation algorithms better explain outcomes than static value algorithms, consistent with OpenEval's assessment of converging evidence.

Perfect agreement on ceDDM modeling (C35-C39, C71-C72). Both evaluations support the model's ability to reproduce empirical patterns. Reviewers describe ceDDM as 'novel' and note authors 'generated surrogate data to demonstrate robustness,' aligning with OpenEval's assessment that the model provides mechanistic account of revaluation-like effects, though both acknowledge it as proof-of-principle.

Strong agreement on study limitations (C88-C90, C93-C94). Both evaluations treat acknowledgment of limitations as appropriate scientific practice. Reviewers explicitly praise authors for 'avoid[ing] over-selling the work, with a lucid description of limitations,' treating this as a strength. OpenEval similarly notes these are reasonable caveats that identify important future research directions without undermining main findings.

Strong agreement on replication analyses (C29-C33). Both evaluations support the partial replication across datasets as strengthening confidence. Reviewers note authors 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon in several existing datasets,' treating replication as evidence of robustness. Both accept the mixed result in one dataset (C33) with the authors' explanation (C91) without challenge.

Strong agreement on neural evidence (C25-C27). Both evaluations support that d-values vs s-values show differential effects in vmPFC. Reviewers explicitly state 'BOLD signal in the vmPFC are better explained by algorithms that update subjective values' and describe evidence as 'solid.' OpenEval notes the fMRI results provide neural evidence supporting behavioral findings, though suggests more detail about confounds would be beneficial.

Strong agreement on control analyses (C19, C69, C20-C21). Both evaluations affirm that control simulations and forward-backward comparisons rule out methodological artifacts. Reviewers note authors 'provided evidence using several techniques and generated surrogate data to demonstrate robustness of their methods,' treating controls as convincing validation. OpenEval similarly assesses these analyses appropriately test the null hypothesis of static values.

Agreement on basic behavioral observations (C3, C8). Both evaluations support the 64% choice consistency finding and its contextualization. Reviewers treat these as establishing context for main findings about dynamic values without questioning the observations. OpenEval notes the low consistency rate is a key observation motivating the study's hypothesis about dynamic values.

Agreement on choice-based model superiority (C60-C61). Both evaluations support that choice-based models outperform s-values. Reviewers accept the limited predictive power of static values without critique. OpenEval notes the superiority is demonstrated empirically through model comparison in Figure 2 and control simulations.

Agreement on asymmetric revaluation (C23, C87). Both evaluations support the empirical finding without challenge. Reviewers do not question the asymmetry and treat it as consistent with established attention patterns. OpenEval notes the asymmetric revaluation is a robust empirical observation, though the mechanistic explanation remains speculative.

Agreement on CIPC contextualization (C73-C76). Both evaluations support the distinction from Chen and Risen artifact and situating findings within CIPC literature. Reviewers explicitly state 'there is a long-standing idea that choices influence evaluation' and affirm the demonstration of re-evaluation phenomenon. OpenEval notes the forward-backward analysis well-supports the distinction from prior artifacts.

Partial overlap on forward-backward analysis (C20-C21). Both evaluations support these claims as part of broader control analyses. Peer review R3 covers C19-C21 and C69 together, while OpenEval R7 covers C20-C21 with C68 and C74. Both affirm the forward-backward comparison provides strong evidence against static values.

OpenEval evaluates theoretical background and motivation (C40-C51) as supported literature review and conceptual framing. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these theoretical claims, though peer reviewers acknowledge the overall theoretical contribution.

OpenEval evaluates the study's central hypothesis (C52-C54) as appropriate and testable hypothesis generation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing the hypothesis formulation, though reviewers affirm the overall research approach.

OpenEval evaluates competing theoretical frameworks (C57-C59) as appropriate contextualization within ongoing debates. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these theoretical frameworks from the literature.

OpenEval evaluates theoretical interpretation and model contextualization (C78-C83) as supported, noting appropriate scientific humility about ceDDM as proxy. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these theoretical interpretation claims.

OpenEval evaluates broader context and connections to related phenomena (C95-C101) as appropriately situating the work within cognitive science, though connections remain somewhat speculative. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these broader contextual claims.
